passages.t: A covenant read aloud, and a land cleared
passages.happening:
Josiah gathers the elders and goes up to the house of the LORD with all the people of Judah and Jerusalem, priests and prophets, ‘all the people small and great’ (verse 2). In their hearing he reads all the words of the Book of the Covenant. Standing by the pillar, he makes a covenant before the LORD to follow him and keep his commandments ‘with all his heart and all his soul’ (verse 3). ‘And all the people entered into the covenant’ (verse 3).

Then the clearing begins. The articles made for Baal, Asherah and the host of heaven are carried out of the temple and burned in the Kidron fields (verse 4). Josiah removes the priests the kings had appointed to burn incense to Baal, the sun, the moon and the stars (verse 5). He burns the Asherah pole from the house of the LORD and grinds it to powder (verse 6). He tears down the quarters of the male shrine prostitutes in the temple (verse 7). He brings the priests of Judah's high places to Jerusalem and defiles the high places from Geba to Beersheba (verse 8). He defiles Topheth in the Valley of Ben-hinnom ‘so that no one could sacrifice his son or daughter in the fire to Molech’ (verse 10). He removes the horses dedicated to the sun and burns the chariots of the sun (verse 11), pulls down the rooftop altars and Manasseh's altars in the temple courts (verse 12), and defiles the high places Solomon had built east of Jerusalem for Ashtoreth, Chemosh and Milcom (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
In chapter 22 the book was found and Huldah announced judgment on Jerusalem and mercy for Josiah. This chapter shows what the king did with the time he was given. It is the most thorough reform in the history of Israel or Judah, and it reaches back through the whole story, to the high places Solomon built and the altar Jeroboam set up.

The reform begins not with destruction but with covenant renewal: the word read aloud to everyone, small and great, and the king and people pledging themselves to it. The word covenant, berit, comes five times in the chapter.

The reform touched almost every kind of worship Judah had taken in. The sun god was sometimes pictured riding a chariot across the sky, which explains the horses and chariots of the sun. Topheth, in the Valley of Ben-hinnom just south of Jerusalem, was where children were burned in sacrifice to Molech, a god whose identity is debated. Josiah made it unclean so that no one could do it again. The text names the practice to say it was ended, and does not describe it. Because of what was done there, the valley's name became a byword for judgment, and in later Jewish usage Ge-hinnom became Gehenna, the word Jesus used for the place of final judgment.

Contact with the dead made a place unclean and unfit for worship, which is why Josiah burned bones on altars and scattered dust on graves. The priests of Judah's high places came to Jerusalem and shared the priests' food, but did not serve at the altar, a middle position between full service and removal.
passages.later: Jeremiah, preaching in these years, said of Topheth that it would be called ‘the Valley of Slaughter’ (Jeremiah 7:32).
passages.asks: Josiah's reform began with reading God's word aloud to everyone, small and great. Ask what part hearing Scripture together plays in renewing a church or a life. And ask what rooftop altars, private and half-forgotten, God's word would reach in yours.

passages.happening:
Josiah pulls down the altar at Bethel, the high place Jeroboam set up, and burns it (verse 15). Seeing tombs on the hillside, he has bones taken out and burned on the altar to defile it, ‘according to the word of the LORD proclaimed by the man of God who had foretold these things’ (verse 16). He asks about a monument and is told it is the tomb of that man of God from Judah. “Let him rest,” he says (verse 18), and the bones are left alone.

In the cities of Samaria he removes the shrines of the high places, and on their altars he kills the priests of the high places and burns human bones (verses 19-20). Back in Jerusalem he commands the people to keep the Passover as written in the Book of the Covenant. ‘No such Passover had been observed from the days of the judges’ (verse 22). He removes the mediums and spiritists, the household gods and idols (verse 24).

‘Neither before nor after Josiah was there any king like him, who turned to the LORD with all his heart and with all his soul and with all his strength, according to all the Law of Moses’ (verse 25). ‘Nevertheless, the LORD did not turn away from the fury of His burning anger, which was kindled against Judah because of all that Manasseh had done’ (verse 26). The LORD will remove Judah as he removed Israel, and reject the city he chose and the temple where he set his Name (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
The reform began in Josiah's eighteenth year, about 622 BC. The scene at Bethel pauses the list to show prophecy fulfilled. About three centuries earlier a man of God from Judah had cried against Jeroboam's altar that a son of David named Josiah would burn bones on it.

The Passover remembered Israel's rescue from Egypt. Deuteronomy required it to be kept at the one place the LORD would choose, rather than in homes and villages, and Josiah's Passover in Jerusalem follows that pattern.

Verse 25 is the narrator's verdict, and it echoes the great command to love the LORD with all one's heart, soul and strength. Then the word Nevertheless turns everything. The verb turn, shuv, the Old Testament's main word for repentance, holds the tension: the king turned to the LORD with all his heart, and the LORD did not turn from his anger. One generation's repentance, however sincere, did not cancel the judgment built up over generations.
passages.later: The man of God had cried at Bethel, ‘A son named Josiah will be born to the house of David’ (1 Kings 13:2). The law said, ‘And you shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength’ (Deuteronomy 6:5), and Jesus called it the first and greatest commandment (Matthew 22:37-38).
passages.hard:
How should a reader take Josiah's killing of the priests of the high places?

Verse 20 says that in the cities of the former northern kingdom Josiah killed the priests of the high places on their altars. It is a violent act, and readers are right to feel its weight. The text tells it in a single verse, and these notes do not dwell on it. Several things place it. Deuteronomy prescribed death for those who led Israel into the worship of other gods, and the text presents Josiah as enforcing the covenant law he had just read. The act also fulfilled the word spoken at Bethel three centuries before. And Josiah treated the priests of Judah's high places differently, bringing them to Jerusalem rather than killing them, which suggests the northern priests were seen as priests of other gods rather than of the LORD.

Christians read such passages in light of the whole Bible. The New Testament gives the church no sword in matters of worship, and Jesus rebuked the disciples who wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village. The chapter shows how seriously the old covenant took idolatry, but it is not a model for how anyone today should treat those who worship differently. It gives no one a warrant to harm, threaten or silence anyone over religion.
passages.asks: Josiah turned to the LORD with everything he had, and the judgment still came. Ask how you hold on to faithfulness when it does not bring the outcome you hoped for. And ask what it would mean to love God with all your heart, soul and strength in the time you have been given.

passages.t: Josiah dies at Megiddo, and Egypt rules
passages.happening:
‘At the end of Josiah’s reign, Pharaoh Neco king of Egypt marched up to help the king of Assyria at the Euphrates River. King Josiah went out to confront him, but Neco faced him and killed him at Megiddo’ (verse 29). His servants carry his body in a chariot to Jerusalem and bury him in his own tomb. The people of the land anoint his son Jehoahaz king (verse 30).

Jehoahaz is twenty-three and reigns three months, doing evil (verses 31-32). Neco imprisons him at Riblah in the land of Hamath and lays a levy on Judah of a hundred talents of silver and a talent of gold (verse 33). Neco makes another son of Josiah, Eliakim, king, and changes his name to Jehoiakim. He takes Jehoahaz to Egypt, where he dies (verse 34). Jehoiakim taxes the land to pay Pharaoh (verse 35). He is twenty-five when he becomes king, reigns eleven years in Jerusalem, and does evil (verses 36-37).
passages.hearers:
Assyria was collapsing. Nineveh fell to the Babylonians and Medes in 612 BC, and what was left of the Assyrian government retreated to Harran. In 609 BC Pharaoh Neco II marched north to support Assyria against Babylon, since Egypt preferred a weak Assyria to a strong Babylon. The Babylonian Chronicle, cuneiform tablets recording events year by year, confirms an Egyptian army coming to Assyria's aid that year. Why Josiah went out to face Neco at Megiddo is not said. Many historians think he sided with Babylon, or wanted to keep Egypt from ruling the region. Chronicles gives a fuller account of the battle.

After Josiah's death Egypt controlled Judah for a few years. Jehoahaz is called Shallum in Jeremiah. Jehoiakim reigned about 609 to 598 BC and paid his tribute by taxing the people. Jeremiah's book shows his reign up close, including the day he burned Jeremiah's scroll.

The energy of the reform drains out of the story. The last verses return to brief royal formulas, as Judah passes into foreign hands.
passages.later: Chronicles says that ‘Jeremiah lamented over Josiah’ (2 Chronicles 35:25). Jeremiah told the people, ‘Do not weep for the dead king; do not mourn his loss. Weep bitterly for the one who is exiled’ (Jeremiah 22:10), meaning Jehoahaz, taken to Egypt.
passages.asks: The best of kings died in a battle he chose, and his sons undid his work. Ask what in your life will outlast you, and what will not. And ask whom you are preparing to carry on what you care about most.
